items.quantitative_outcome: NTT raised the success rate in a vulnerability-analysis benchmark evaluation by 15 percentage points, from 48% with the conventional method to 63%.
items.signal: A measured benchmark improvement tied to NTT’s proprietary vulnerability-research-informed analysis workflow; the approach also analyzes source code without sending it to external AI services. This is a candidate signal, not evidence of durable competitive advantage.

items.comparator: Claude Code powered by Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI Codex based on GPT-5.6 Cyber: both 45.3% accuracy on the reported benchmark
items.quantitative_outcome: Cogent Security’s VR-1.1 scored 57.9% accuracy across 190 Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures on LiveCVEBench.
items.signal: The reported benchmark result suggests stronger vulnerability-finding and remediation accuracy, but the same report says successful tasks averaged about 2.23 million tokens and 31 turns, versus roughly 380,000 tokens and 8.4 turns for Claude Code. Advantage is therefore uncertain, particularly on efficiency.

items.comparator: GPT-5.6 Cyber: 32.1% on ExploitGym; GPT-6 Astra: 32.0% vulnerability recall in OpenAI’s separate web-penetration evaluation
items.quantitative_outcome: GPT-6 Cyber scored 48.5% on ExploitGym, up from 32.1% for GPT-5.6 Cyber. In a separate web-penetration evaluation, it achieved 40.3% vulnerability recall compared with 32.0% for GPT-6 Astra.
items.signal: OpenAI reports measurable gains on its cybersecurity benchmarks. These are model capability results, not demonstrated operating benefits for a cybersecurity or defense company, so they are a weaker fit for the requested competitive-advantage screen.
